messages.content: You are an experienced power-plant performance engineer. Answer with a single JSON object and nothing else.

A combined cycle power plant has one gas turbine, a heat recovery steam generator and a steam turbine. It runs at full load. Hourly records give net electrical output (MW) together with ambient temperature (2 to 37 degC), ambient pressure, relative humidity and condenser vacuum. The plant has no inlet cooling, and over this ambient range the gas turbine stays below the rated limit of its generator. On cold, humid days an inlet anti-icing system heats the intake air with compressor bleed.

Question: over the 2 to 37 degC ambient range, is there a temperature beyond which the net output responds to ambient temperature differently from elsewhere (much more weakly, or in the opposite direction)? There may be none, one or more on the cold side, one on the hot side, or several.
Reply with JSON only, in this form:
{"boundaries": [{"side": "below" or "above", "at_c": <degC>, "rh_above": <percent, or null>, "mechanism": "power_cap" or "anti_icing" or "evap_cooling" or "other", "output_trend": "rises" or "falls" or "about the same", "confidence": <0 to 1>}], "rationale": "<one or two sentences>"}
"side": "below" means the different response holds below at_c; "above" means above at_c. "rh_above" is the relative humidity above which it applies, or null if it applies at any humidity. "mechanism" names the cause: power_cap is a generator or power limit, anti_icing is inlet anti-icing heating, evap_cooling is inlet evaporative cooling. "output_trend" says how net output changes as ambient temperature moves further beyond at_c. Use an empty list if you expect no such temperature.

response: {"boundaries": [{"side": "below", "at_c": 5, "rh_above": 80, "mechanism": "anti_icing", "output_trend": "about the same", "confidence": 0.9}], "rationale": "Below 5°C and above 80% relative humidity, the anti-icing system activates, heating the intake air and counteracting the expected increase in output from colder temperatures, leading to a flatter or near-constant net output trend."}

Hourly records give net electrical output (MW) together with ambient temperature (2 to 37 degC), ambient pressure, relative humidity and condenser vacuum. The plant has no inlet cooling. In cold weather the gas turbine reaches the rated limit of its generator, and the control system holds it at that limit. On cold, humid days an inlet anti-icing system heats the intake air with compressor bleed.

Question: over the 2 to 37 degC ambient range, is there a temperature beyond which the net output responds to ambient temperature differently from elsewhere (much more weakly, or in the opposite direction)? There may be none, one or more on the cold side, one on the hot side, or several.
Reply with JSON only, in this form:
{"boundaries": [{"side": "below" or "above", "at_c": <degC>, "rh_above": <percent, or null>, "mechanism": "power_cap" or "anti_icing" or "evap_cooling" or "other", "output_trend": "rises" or "falls" or "about the same", "confidence": <0 to 1>}], "rationale": "<one or two sentences>"}
"side": "below" means the different response holds below at_c; "above" means above at_c. "rh_above" is the relative humidity above which it applies, or null if it applies at any humidity. "mechanism" names the cause: power_cap is a generator or power limit, anti_icing is inlet anti-icing heating, evap_cooling is inlet evaporative cooling. "output_trend" says how net output changes as ambient temperature moves further beyond at_c. Use an empty list if you expect no such temperature.

response: {"boundaries": [{"side": "below", "at_c": 5, "rh_above": 80, "mechanism": "anti_icing", "output_trend": "about the same", "confidence": 0.9}], "rationale": "Below 5°C and above 80% relative humidity, the inlet anti-icing system activates, heating the intake air and counteracting the expected increase in output from colder temperatures, resulting in a flatter response to further cooling."}

Hourly records give net electrical output (MW) together with ambient temperature (2 to 37 degC), ambient pressure, relative humidity and condenser vacuum. The plant has no inlet cooling. In cold weather the gas turbine reaches the rated limit of its generator, and the control system holds it at that limit. On cold, humid days an inlet anti-icing system heats the intake air with compressor bleed.
Training data available: 146 hourly records with ambient temperature between 4.5 and 6.9 degC. Within these records a linear fit gives d(output)/d(temperature) = 0.61 MW/degC (standard error 0.60). Predictions are needed outside this temperature range.

Question: over the 2 to 37 degC ambient range, is there a temperature beyond which the net output responds to ambient temperature differently from elsewhere (much more weakly, or in the opposite direction)? There may be none, one or more on the cold side, one on the hot side, or several.
Reply with JSON only, in this form:
{"boundaries": [{"side": "below" or "above", "at_c": <degC>, "rh_above": <percent, or null>, "mechanism": "power_cap" or "anti_icing" or "evap_cooling" or "other", "output_trend": "rises" or "falls" or "about the same", "confidence": <0 to 1>}], "rationale": "<one or two sentences>"}
"side": "below" means the different response holds below at_c; "above" means above at_c. "rh_above" is the relative humidity above which it applies, or null if it applies at any humidity. "mechanism" names the cause: power_cap is a generator or power limit, anti_icing is inlet anti-icing heating, evap_cooling is inlet evaporative cooling. "output_trend" says how net output changes as ambient temperature moves further beyond at_c. Use an empty list if you expect no such temperature.

response: {"boundaries": [{"side": "below", "at_c": 5.0, "rh_above": 80, "mechanism": "anti_icing", "output_trend": "about the same", "confidence": 0.85}], "rationale": "At temperatures below 5.0°C and relative humidity above 80%, the inlet anti-icing system activates, heating the intake air and offsetting the expected increase in output from colder temperatures, resulting in a flatter response compared to the linear trend observed in the training data."}

Hourly records give net electrical output (MW) together with ambient temperature (2 to 37 degC), ambient pressure, relative humidity and condenser vacuum. The plant has no inlet cooling. In cold weather the gas turbine reaches the rated limit of its generator, and the control system holds it at that limit. On cold, humid days an inlet anti-icing system heats the intake air with compressor bleed.
Training data available: 146 hourly records with ambient temperature between 4.5 and 6.9 degC. Within these records a linear fit gives d(output)/d(temperature) = 0.61 MW/degC (standard error 0.60). Predictions are needed outside this temperature range.

Question: over the 2 to 37 degC ambient range, is there a temperature beyond which the net output responds to ambient temperature differently from elsewhere (much more weakly, or in the opposite direction)? There may be none, one or more on the cold side, one on the hot side, or several.
Reply with JSON only, in this form:
{"boundaries": [{"side": "below" or "above", "at_c": <degC>, "rh_above": <percent, or null>, "mechanism": "power_cap" or "anti_icing" or "evap_cooling" or "other", "output_trend": "rises" or "falls" or "about the same", "confidence": <0 to 1>}], "rationale": "<one or two sentences>"}
"side": "below" means the different response holds below at_c; "above" means above at_c. "rh_above" is the relative humidity above which it applies, or null if it applies at any humidity. "mechanism" names the cause: power_cap is a generator or power limit, anti_icing is inlet anti-icing heating, evap_cooling is inlet evaporative cooling. "output_trend" says how net output changes as ambient temperature moves further beyond at_c. Use an empty list if you expect no such temperature.

response: {"boundaries": [{"side": "below", "at_c": 5.0, "rh_above": 80, "mechanism": "anti_icing", "output_trend": "about the same", "confidence": 0.85}], "rationale": "At temperatures below 5°C and high humidity (>80%), the inlet anti-icing system activates, heating the intake air and counteracting the expected increase in output with cooling, leading to a flatter response to further temperature decreases."}

Hourly records give net electrical output (MW) together with ambient temperature (2 to 37 degC), ambient pressure, relative humidity and condenser vacuum. The plant has no inlet cooling. In cold weather the gas turbine reaches the rated limit of its generator, and the control system holds it at that limit. On cold, humid days an inlet anti-icing system heats the intake air with compressor bleed.
Training data available: 146 hourly records with ambient temperature between 31.3 and 33.8 degC. Within these records a linear fit gives d(output)/d(temperature) = -2.38 MW/degC (standard error 0.67). Predictions are needed outside this temperature range.

Question: over the 2 to 37 degC ambient range, is there a temperature beyond which the net output responds to ambient temperature differently from elsewhere (much more weakly, or in the opposite direction)? There may be none, one or more on the cold side, one on the hot side, or several.
Reply with JSON only, in this form:
{"boundaries": [{"side": "below" or "above", "at_c": <degC>, "rh_above": <percent, or null>, "mechanism": "power_cap" or "anti_icing" or "evap_cooling" or "other", "output_trend": "rises" or "falls" or "about the same", "confidence": <0 to 1>}], "rationale": "<one or two sentences>"}
"side": "below" means the different response holds below at_c; "above" means above at_c. "rh_above" is the relative humidity above which it applies, or null if it applies at any humidity. "mechanism" names the cause: power_cap is a generator or power limit, anti_icing is inlet anti-icing heating, evap_cooling is inlet evaporative cooling. "output_trend" says how net output changes as ambient temperature moves further beyond at_c. Use an empty list if you expect no such temperature.

response: {"boundaries": [{"side": "below", "at_c": 10, "rh_above": 80, "mechanism": "anti_icing", "output_trend": "about the same", "confidence": 0.9}], "rationale": "On cold, humid days, inlet anti-icing heating is activated above 80% relative humidity, which counteracts the cooling benefit of low temperatures and stabilizes output, causing the response to ambient temperature to weaken below 10°C."}
